entities.name: Miguel Corte-Real
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Miguel Corte-Real, a scion of the influential Portuguese Corte-Real family of explorers, was a pivotal figure in the early 16th-century Portuguese quest for a Northwest Passage and new fishing grounds in the North Atlantic. Operating under the patronage of King Manuel I, his expeditions between 1500 and 1502 significantly extended European knowledge of the North American coastline, particularly along the eastern shores of what is now Canada. Though his ultimate fate remains shrouded in mystery, his voyages contributed to the nascent mapping of the New World and underscored Portugal's ambitious, albeit ultimately less successful than Spain's, engagement with transatlantic exploration. His efforts were part of a broader European scramble to claim new territories and resources following Columbus's initial discoveries.

Miguel's defining expedition commenced in May 1502, when he departed Lisbon with three caravels, intending to locate his missing brother Gaspar, who had vanished on a similar quest the previous year. Miguel's fleet reached the coasts of present-day Labrador and Newfoundland, charting approximately 600 miles of shoreline and encountering indigenous peoples, some of whom were reportedly captured. The expedition divided to cover more ground, and Miguel's vessel, after agreeing to rendezvous, was never seen again. The other two ships returned to Portugal in the autumn of 1502, bringing news of the discoveries and the grim disappearance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Miguel Corte-Real's expeditions contributed to early European cartography of North America, particularly the coasts of Labrador and Newfoundland, and his disappearance, along with his brother's, significantly altered the trajectory of Portuguese colonial ambitions in the region.
